facts.t: The judiciary is writing AI rules before adopting AI at scale
facts.d: The Supreme Court's AI Committee released draft Regulations for public consultation in June 2026 — an unusual sequence. Architecture decided now will be very hard to reverse once systems are embedded, which is why the Committee treats it as a constitutional moment.

facts.t: Some AI uses are absolutely prohibited, not merely regulated
facts.d: Risk-scoring for flight risk, predicting recidivism, assessing bail eligibility, judging witness credibility and any black-box system touching personal liberty. These are non-derogable bars, not conditions.

facts.t: India has no UIDAI for the courts
facts.d: UPI got NPCI and Aadhaar got UIDAI — permanent, resourced institutions. Court technology has produced a succession of committees with rotating membership instead, which is why every reform list begins with consolidating them into one durable body.

bank.q: Which tool translates judgments into eighteen languages?
bank.e: SUVAS. SUPACE handles precedent identification, LegRAA legal research, and PANINI translation and linguistic structuring.

bank.q: With reference to the Draft Regulations, 2026, consider the following statements:
s: Lawyers must disclose AI assistance in drafting pleadings.
Courts must inform litigants where AI materially assists a judge.
AI-generated output may be submitted as independent evidence if disclosed.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Submitting AI output as independent evidence is absolutely prohibited, disclosed or not.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT among the absolute prohibitions?
bank.e: Transcription is an operational, permitted use. The other three touch liberty and judgement, and are barred outright.

bank.q: Match List I (country) with List II (initiative):
pairs: 1. VICTOR at the Federal Supreme Court
2. Guidelines for Use of AI in Canadian Courts, 2024
3. Smart Courts and the Hangzhou Internet Court
bank.e: China's Smart Courts, Brazil's VICTOR, Singapore's small claims guidance, and the Canadian Judicial Council's 2024 guidelines.

bank.as: The Apex Body overseeing judicial AI faces a conflict-of-interest objection.
bank.rs: It is appointed predominantly by sitting judges of the very judiciary it regulates.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — hence the proposal to include independent technologists, civil society and the Bar.

bank.q: Consider the following statements about institutional architecture:
s: CoRE-AI is intended to be a neutral research body with no procurement stake.
Each court is to have an AI Secretariat headed by a District Judge-level officer.
Cyber Security is one of the five specialised committees.
bank.e: All three are correct. The others are Judicial, Technical, Infrastructure and Finance, and Case and Data Management.

bank.q: Which American controversy is cited as the cautionary example of algorithmic bias?
bank.e: The COMPAS recidivism-scoring controversy — the reason recidivism prediction is absolutely prohibited in the Indian draft.

bank.q: All of the following are contested issues in the draft framework EXCEPT:
o: Absence of uniform mandatory technical standards across High Courts
SCAORA's opposition to the blanket AI-disclosure requirement
An undefined interface with the national AI-governance framework
An excess of permanent, well-resourced execution bodies
bank.e: The complaint is the absence of any such body — the judiciary has committees with rotating membership rather than a permanent institution.

bank.q: The e-Courts Phase III outlay, including its Future Technological Advancement component, is:
bank.e: ₹7,210 crore across 2023 to 2027, with a specific component for AI, machine learning and blockchain.

bank.q: With reference to constitutional anchors for judicial AI regulation, consider the following:
s: Article 21's guarantee of speedy trial justifies efficiency-enhancing technology.
Articles 141 and 145 supply the basis for the Supreme Court to frame regulations.
Courts fall squarely within the enforcement architecture of the DPDP Act, 2023.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Courts largely sit outside the DPDP Act's direct enforcement architecture, which is why a specific judicial data protocol is proposed.

bank.q: Which reform proposes separating the standard-setter from market participants?
o: Placing prohibitions on a statutory footing
Insulating CoRE-AI from procurement and vendor relationships
Scaling multilingual tools to district courts
bank.e: The UPI-style separation — a body that sets standards must not also have a stake in procuring the systems it approves.

bank.as: Efficiency gains from court technology can disadvantage some litigants.
bank.rs: E-filing and virtual hearings presuppose literacy, devices and connectivity that many litigants lack.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — which is why continued offline access through e-Seva Kendras and legal services authorities is part of the recommendation.
